title: What Sells on Vinted: Real Sold-Price Data & the Brands That Hold Value (2026)
intro: Vinted doesn't show sold prices, so most advice about what sells on it is guesswork. This page is different — it's based on real sold prices collected from actual Vinted sales, showing which brands sell most often, what they actually go for, and which categories hold their value best.

body.heading: Why this data is different
paragraphs: Almost everything written about "what sells on Vinted" is opinion, because Vinted deliberately hides sold prices — there's no completed-listings view, unlike eBay. The best most guides can do is look at *asking* prices, which are what hopeful sellers want, not what buyers actually pay.

The figures below come from real completed sales — items that were listed, watched, and confirmed sold. That's the difference between "what people are asking" and "what people are paying", and it's the difference between pricing to sell and pricing to wait.

This data is collected automatically as items sell, across a spread of brands and categories. It isn't a complete picture of every sale on Vinted — it's a representative sample of what actually moves, which is enough to spot the patterns that matter.

body.heading: The brands that sell most often
paragraphs: Based on real completed sales, these are the brands that move most frequently. The pattern is consistent: well-known names with a loyal second-hand following dominate, because buyers search for them by name.
• **Ralph Lauren** — one of the highest-volume sellers, driven by polo shirts, knitwear and casual wear at accessible prices.
• **The North Face** — outerwear and fleeces, a brand buyers actively hunt for second-hand.
• **LEGO** — a category, not a brand, but it behaves like one: sets, minifigures and bulk lots sell constantly.
• **Carhartt** — workwear and streetwear, with a strong resale culture.
• **Pokémon** — cards and merch, a surprisingly high-volume second-hand market.
• **Barbour** — the standout for *value retention* (see below), not just volume.
• **Stone Island, Moncler, Lululemon, Nike, Dr. Martens** — all steady sellers with dedicated buyers.

The common thread: every one of these is a brand people search for *by name*. Unbranded clothing sells, but it doesn't get found the way a "Barbour jacket" search does. If you're sourcing to resell, brand recognition is the single biggest predictor of whether something moves.

body.heading: What things actually sell for
paragraphs: This is where the real data surprises people. The *average* price is often low because it mixes a few high-value items with a lot of small ones — so here are the ranges instead, which tell the honest story:
• **Barbour** — the widest spread: from a few pounds for a t-shirt up to £220 for a waxed jacket. Jackets hold value; the clothing-line basics don't.
• **LEGO** — from a couple of pounds for small sets to £100+ for large or retiring sets. Set size and retirement status drive the price far more than condition.
• **Dr. Martens** — £8 to £100, with genuine vintage Made-in-England pairs at the top end.
• **Nike** — £4 to £30 for trainers, with rare or hyped colourways going well above that.
• **The North Face** — £1 to £48, with vintage or limited pieces above that.
• **Stone Island, Moncler, Lululemon** — often lower than people expect, because the high-street-casual lines outnumber the rare pieces.

The lesson isn't a single number — it's that *within any brand, the specific item* determines the price. A Barbour t-shirt and a Barbour jacket are the same brand but a 20x price difference. That's why a sold-price tool that shows you the actual item, not a category average, is the only useful guide. Read [how to see sold prices on Vinted](/guides/how-to-see-sold-prices-on-vinted) for exactly how this works.

body.heading: Which items hold value best
paragraphs: Three patterns emerge from the sold data, and they're the real insight for anyone buying to resell or selling their own wardrobe:

1. **Outerwear beats basics.** Barbour jackets, North Face fleeces and Carhartt jackets hold value; the t-shirts and polos with the same logo sell for single figures. Buyers pay for the functional item, not the label alone.

2. **Toys and collectibles are the sleeper category.** LEGO and Pokémon sell constantly and hold value well, because sets and cards have objective scarcity — a retired set or a rare card has a floor that a worn t-shirt doesn't.

3. **Brand + condition + specific model, in that order.** A genuine vintage Dr. Martens 1460 in good condition is worth far more than a generic newer pair. The more specific the item, the more it holds value — which is exactly why [alerting on specific items rather than broad brands](/guides/vinted-price-alert) is how serious buyers catch these.

For sellers, the takeaway is simple: if you have outerwear, toys or well-known branded pieces, they're worth listing properly with good photos and specific titles. If you have unbranded basics, price them to move — they're competing with everything else that looks identical.

body.heading: What this means for buying on Vinted
paragraphs: If you're buying, the sold data tells you where the genuine deals are. The brands that sell most often are also the ones where new listings appear most often — which means the good prices go within minutes. A Barbour jacket priced at the bottom of its range doesn't sit; it gets snapped up.

That's the practical problem a saved-search alert solves: the moment a specific item in your size and price range is listed, you know about it. Waiting to check manually means someone else got there first. [Set an alert for the items you actually want](/guides/vinted-price-alert) and you're buying at the sold-price reality, not the asking-price optimism.

body.heading: The honest caveat about averages
paragraphs: A word of caution that most data articles skip: never price an item off a brand's *average* sold price. Averages are meaningless across a whole brand, because they mix £5 t-shirts with £220 jackets. A Barbour "average" of around £20 would have you pricing a waxed jacket ten times too low.

The only price signal that matters is the *specific item* — the model, the condition, and what comparable pieces actually sold for. That's why this page shows ranges and patterns rather than a single misleading number, and why the [sold-price tool](/guides/how-to-see-sold-prices-on-vinted) reports the actual item, not a category average.

This data is a live snapshot and grows as more sales are recorded. The patterns — outerwear holds value, toys are the sleeper category, brand recognition drives volume — are stable; the specific prices move with the market.

faq.question: What sells best on Vinted?
faq.answer: Well-known brands with a loyal second-hand following — Ralph Lauren, The North Face, Carhartt, Barbour, Nike, Dr. Martens — plus LEGO and Pokémon, which are the sleeper collectible categories. The common thread is that buyers search for these by name, so they get found.

faq.question: Do brands hold their value on Vinted?
faq.answer: Outerwear and specific models do — Barbour jackets, North Face fleeces and vintage Dr. Martens hold value far better than the t-shirts and basics with the same logo. Toys and collectibles (LEGO, Pokémon) also hold value well because of objective scarcity.

faq.question: Why is the average price misleading on Vinted?
faq.answer: A brand average mixes cheap basics with high-value pieces — a Barbour t-shirt at £5 and a waxed jacket at £220 average out to a meaningless number. The only useful price signal is the specific item, model and condition, which is why a sold-price tool that shows the actual item matters.

faq.question: Is this data all the sales on Vinted?
faq.answer: No — it's a representative sample of real completed sales collected automatically as items sell, not a complete record of every transaction. It's enough to spot reliable patterns (which brands move, which items hold value), but not a census.
